record.paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
record.original_question: Is the class of orderable groups the axiomatic closure of the class of O*-groups, where an O*-group is a group in which every partial order extends to a total order making the group totally ordered?

evidence.quote: 3.17∗ . (A.I. Kokorin [83] Problem 3.20) Is the class of orderable groups the axiomatic closure of the class O ∗?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Call a group $G$ orderable if there exists a total order $\le$ on $G$ that is bi-invariant, i.e. $a\le b$ implies $xay\le xby$ for all $x,y\in G$. Call a partial order $\preceq$ on $G$ a partial group order if it is invariant under left and right multiplication. Define an O*-group to be a group $G$ with the property that every partial group order on $G$ extends to a total bi-invariant order on $G$.

A class $\mathcal{K}$ of groups is said to be axiomatically closed (or to be the axiomatic closure of a subclass $\mathcal{K}_0\subseteq\mathcal{K}$) if $\mathcal{K}$ consists of exactly those groups that satisfy every first-order sentence in the language of groups that holds in every member of $\mathcal{K}_0$.

Question: Is the class of orderable groups equal to the axiomatic closure of the class of O*-groups?
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is recorded as Kokorin's Problem 3.20 and is listed among unsolved problems on ordered and orderable groups. Related results (e.g., Bludov's theorem that the axiomatic rank of the quasivariety of orderable groups is infinite) bear on the structure of axiomatic descriptions of orderable groups but do not appear to resolve this specific question. No source found that announces a resolution.
